newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle set to blast off with oldest astronaut.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle set to blast off with oldest astronaut.

text.p: The shuttle Columbia was set for blastoff on Tuesday carrying a five-member crew that includes NASA's oldest astronaut, space agency officials said on Monday.

Columbia was scheduled to roar away at 2:53 p.m. EST (1953 GMT) on Tuesday. Florida launch pad workers reported no major technical problems with the $2 billion spaceship. "We're on track and everything's going very well," shuttle test director John Guidi said.

The crew of five astronauts includes Story Musgrave, who at 61 years old will become the oldest spaceflier ever. This will be his sixth trip in orbit, equalling the record currently held by veteran astronaut and moonwalker John Young.
"When Story started in the space business many of us were school age or less," said Columbia commander Ken Cockrell.

Musgrave joined the astronaut corps in 1967 and waited 16 years for his first trip into space. With this mission he will have flown on all five of NASA's shuttle orbiters. In 1993 he was one of four spacewalking astronauts who carried out a delicate repair on NASA's Hubble Space Telescope.
The main goal of Columbia's 16-day flight, the 80th shuttle mission, will be the release and later recovery of two science satellites.

The first, Orfeus-Spas, will be dropped off using the shuttle's robot arm seven hours after launch. The observatory will fly free of Columbia for two weeks studying the mysterious matter between the stars.

The second craft, the Wake Shield Facility, will test an innovative process for manufacturing ultra-pure semiconductors in the vacuum of space. The University of Houston and Space Industries Inc., which designed and built the flying saucer-shaped craft, say they have fixed technical problems that dogged two earlier test flights.

Astronauts Tom Jones and Tammy Jernigan plan a pair of spacewalks to practice construction of the planned international space station. Their work outside will include a test of a manually operated crane for moving large space station components.

U.S. Air Force meteorologists predicted an 80 percent chance of acceptable weather for launch. They expected dry conditions and little wind. "We should be good shape for getting off the ground tomorrow," shuttle weather officer Ed Priselac told a news conference on Monday.

NASA managers were, however, monitoring high seas off Cape Canaveral where the shuttle's booster rockets will splash down for recovery and reuse, Priselac said. Swells of 16 feet (4.5 metres) may prevent NASA's booster recovery ships from leaving port.
The shuttle's liftoff had been scheduled for Friday but countdown clocks had been on hold since last Wednesday because of stormy weather.
Columbia, NASA's oldest shuttle, is due to return to earth at the Kennedy Space Centre on Dec. 5.
